caption:
Loan filings reviewed by Bloomberg show a Nvidia GB300 NVL72 rack, 72 Blackwell Ultra chips, at a Shanghai data center tied to Alice Huang.
A Chinese firm pledged it as collateral for a $14 million loan. Blackwell chips have always needed a US license to go to China.
Jensen Huang once said racks like this were too big to smuggle.

How do you think a 1,500 kg rack got there?

site_article.seo_description: Bloomberg found a Nvidia GB300 rack with 72 Blackwell chips pledged for a $14 million loan at a Shanghai data center tied to Megaspeed founder Alice Huang.
site_article.answer_summary: Bloomberg reported that Chinese loan filings place a Nvidia GB300 NVL72 rack, with 72 Blackwell Ultra chips, at a Shanghai data center tied to Alice Huang. How the rack reached China is not known, and Bloomberg found no evidence that Megaspeed sent it.

paragraphs.text: A Nvidia GB300 NVL72 server rack has turned up at a Shanghai data center linked to Alice Huang, the founder of Singapore based Megaspeed, according to a Bloomberg report published on November 27, 2026. Bloomberg found the hardware in loan documents that two Chinese companies submitted to regulators, and said the filings are the first documentary evidence that Blackwell chips reached a data center tied to Huang and Megaspeed.

According to Bloomberg, a company called Shanghai Shuoyao offered the GB300 NVL72 rack as collateral for a 96 million yuan loan, about $14 million, from Shanghai Innovation Bank. The rack's serial number appeared in documents filed in November. A GB300 NVL72 rack holds 72 Blackwell Ultra chips and 36 Grace processors, stands about two meters tall and can weigh more than 1,500 kilograms.

A second company, Shanghai Kezhan, described a GB200 server at the same facility when it took a 90 million yuan loan in late 2025 from a finance leasing firm wholly owned by a Shanghai government agency, Bloomberg reported. Kezhan also listed 32 servers with H200 chips. Bloomberg said some Chinese lenders, including ones with government ties, have lent against restricted Nvidia hardware.

Bloomberg ran the rack's serial number through a public warranty database, which showed it was built by Taiwan's Gigabyte Technology. Gigabyte declined to say who first bought it, citing company policy, and said it conducts all business in compliance with applicable laws and regulations. How the rack reached China is not known. Bloomberg noted that such equipment often passes through several hands.

Alice Huang founded Megaspeed in 2023, and it became Nvidia's largest customer in Southeast Asia, according to Bloomberg. The Trump administration put Megaspeed on a US trade blacklist this month, citing a significant risk of chip diversion. Megaspeed is under US investigation over suspected smuggling and has denied wrongdoing.

Shuoyao has confirmed it provides services to Megaspeed and described the relationship as ordinary commercial cooperation. Kezhan is 83.3 percent owned by NeXPower Japan, a Tokyo firm that Caixin has said Alice Huang controls, Bloomberg reported. Megaspeed used a 2024 rendering of the Shanghai project, which Bloomberg calls the Yangtze River Delta Project, to show investors its largest data center. Local media say the site could hold up to 800,000 servers.
Bloomberg said it has no evidence that Megaspeed itself sent Nvidia hardware to the site. Neither Megaspeed nor Nvidia answered Bloomberg's questions about the project.

Blackwell chips have always required a US license to ship to China, and President Trump has said he does not want them going there, Bloomberg reported. Jensen Huang once said a GB300 rack was too big to smuggle. The report comes days after Nvidia reinstated Huang as chief executive, according to The Next Web.

The filings matter because they are paper evidence rather than rumor. A rack of this size and value sitting in a Shanghai facility, and accepted by a bank as collateral, suggests that restricted hardware can move through resellers and still be treated as an ordinary financial asset once it arrives. That puts pressure on Nvidia's long standing position that its products do not leak into a black market, and on the export rules meant to keep them out.
Watch whether US export officials trace the serial number back to the first buyer, and whether Nvidia or Gigabyte explain how the rack left their supply chain.
